# Artifact Keeper 1.7.4

**1.7.4 is a security-only release: four advisories, one commit, no migrations.** On top of 1.7.3 it carries exactly one functional change — the four fixes below, shipped together — plus the version bump. No new features, no schema changes, nothing to plan a window around. If you are already on 1.7.3 this is a small, low-risk upgrade and you can take it quickly; that is the point of cutting it as its own number rather than folding it into the next feature release.

**Three of the four need more than an upgrade**, and all three are easy to miss:

- **GHSA-78h6 may have handed your configured upstream registry credentials to a third party.** If you are inside its precondition, upgrading stops the leak but does not undo it — **rotate those credentials**.
- **GHSA-qxv7 means unverified bytes may already be sitting in your proxy cache.** Upgrading stops new ones being admitted; it does not evict the ones already there, and they will not expire on their own.
- **GHSA-9rqp put callers' tokens inside plugin memory.** If you ran a WASM plugin you did not author, rotate the tokens that were used against its routes.

Both are spelled out under [What to do beyond upgrading](#what-to-do-beyond-upgrading). There is also **one deliberate behaviour change** that will affect Docker Hub pull-through — read [that section](#docker-hub-pull-through-now-authenticates-anonymously) before you deploy if you proxy Docker Hub with credentials.

## Am I affected?

Ordered by severity, not by advisory number.

### 1. Any authenticated caller could read a private repository's artifact inventory through the `/ext` WASM plugin proxy — GHSA-9rqp-mgmw-5879

**The mechanism.** The plugin protocol proxy is mounted at `/ext` and routes as `/ext/<format_key>/<repo_key>/...` — the plugin's format key first, the repository second. Every other format route in Artifact Keeper puts the repository key in the second path segment, and `extract_repo_key`, which the repository-visibility middleware uses to decide *what it is authorizing*, applied that general rule to `/ext` too. It therefore returned the **plugin format key** as the repository key. No repository matched that string, so the middleware fell into its no-repository branch — the branch that exists for routes with no repository in the path. Anonymous callers were still refused there, but **any authenticated caller passed straight through with no visibility check, no permission check and no token-scope check against the repository actually being addressed**. The handler then looked the real repository up itself, performed no authorization of its own, and handed the plugin that repository's entire artifact metadata list.

**Am I affected?** Only if **both** of these hold:

1. you run a WASM plugin that exports the **v2** `request-handler` interface — that is what serves `/ext` at all, and the handler refuses any format key with no such plugin registered, so a v1 plugin is not enough; **and**
2. at least one **non-public** repository was created against that plugin's custom format key.

That second condition bounds the blast radius, and it is worth being precise about: the handler requires the target repository's own format key to equal the plugin's, so what was exposed was private repositories *on a v2-plugin-served format*, not every private repository in the instance. Built-in formats (Maven, npm, PyPI, OCI and the rest) carry no format-key row and were never reachable this way. If you run no v2 protocol plugins, this one did not affect you. Plugin installation is admin-only and signature-verified by default, so this is not a self-service foothold.

**What actually crossed the boundary — and what did not.** The plugin receives the repository's artifact metadata: path, version, content type, size in bytes and SHA-256 digest for every live artifact. That is a full inventory disclosure, and the plugin renders it into whatever the caller asked for (a PEP 503 index, for example). It is **not** artifact content: the plugin interface is handed metadata only, the guest has no network access and no filesystem, and the download URLs a plugin embeds in its index point back at the ordinary REST download route, which enforces visibility independently — so those links `404` for a caller with no grant. There is no write path through this interface either. **Read the impact as unauthorized disclosure of a private repository's artifact inventory, not as artifact theft.**

Two things make the reach wider than "any authenticated caller" suggests, and neither was in the advisory text. The skipped check included the **repository-scope ceiling**, so an API token deliberately restricted to one repository could read another repository's inventory through `/ext`. And the handler's format-key mismatch reply named the repository's actual format (`400`) where a missing repository answered `404` — an existence-and-format oracle over **every repository in the instance**, which did not require the format-key match and so reached much further than the inventory disclosure did. Both are closed by the same middleware fix.

**The fix** is in three parts. `extract_repo_key` now skips the format-key segment on `/ext`, so the middleware evaluates the real repository and applies the standard gate — anonymous gets `401` with the credential challenge, an authenticated caller without a grant gets the existence-hiding `404` the REST path returns, a granted member passes; the token-scope ceiling and the fine-grained ACLs, both inert on `/ext` before, now apply. The handler additionally calls `require_visible` itself rather than trusting the middleware to have parsed the path correctly, and fails closed (`500`) if the access check errors. And separately —

**The same commit closes a second, distinct exposure in the same handler: the caller's own credentials were being copied into plugin memory.** `headers_to_pairs` forwarded *every* client request header into the WASM guest, including `Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `X-API-Key` and `X-NuGet-ApiKey`. A plugin has no legitimate need for any of them. Forwarding is now restricted to an eleven-entry allowlist of benign protocol and content-negotiation headers (`accept`, `accept-encoding`, `accept-language`, `content-length`, `content-type`, `host`, `if-modified-since`, `if-none-match`, `if-range`, `range`, `user-agent`); credential and hop-by-hop headers are never copied. To be accurate about what this means: plugins run sandboxed with no network and no filesystem, so a plugin could *read* those credentials but had no direct channel to send them anywhere except the host's own log stream. If you ran a plugin you do not fully control, see the rotation note below.

### 2. Upstream registry credentials could be forwarded to a cross-origin token realm — GHSA-78h6-3wp8-2542

**The mechanism.** When a proxied pull gets a `401` from its upstream, the upstream names the token endpoint to use in its own `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="..."` header. That realm URL is **upstream-controlled input**. Artifact Keeper validated it against the SSRF rules — which keep the token request off internal and link-local addresses — and then sent the repository's **stored upstream Basic credentials** to whatever public host the realm named. A registry that is hostile, compromised, or able to have its `401` responses tampered with could therefore name an attacker's host as its realm and be handed the username and password the operator configured for that upstream. The realm was permitted to be plain `http://`, so in that case the credentials also went out in cleartext.

**Am I affected?** You need a **remote or proxy repository with upstream Basic credentials configured**. Three narrowings matter:

- **Only Basic credentials leaked.** A configured upstream *bearer token* was never forwarded to the realm — that code path only ever matched the Basic variant.
- **There is no attacker on your side of the connection.** A user of your registry can *trigger* the fetch, but cannot influence the realm. Exploitation requires the upstream registry itself to be hostile or compromised, a TLS interception of it, or a credentialed proxy repository pointed at a registry the operator does not trust. This is not remotely reachable by an unauthenticated caller.
- **The advisory says OCI, and OCI is the realistic case, but the code is format-agnostic** — any upstream that answers `401` with a `Bearer realm=` challenge reached it.

The practical assessment is a configuration review: list your remote/proxy repositories that carry stored upstream credentials, and for each, judge whether someone could have controlled that upstream's `401` response. If every such upstream is a registry you or a trusted vendor operates over TLS, the realistic exposure is low. Where it is not, **rotate** — see below.

**The fix** pins credential forwarding to the configured upstream's **origin** — scheme, host and port, host compared case-insensitively and default ports normalized — the same rule the NuGet feed-resource fetches already use. The baseline is the operator-configured upstream, not the URL of whatever responded, so a redirect cannot move the goalposts. A realm on a different origin gets the token request **without** credentials rather than a hard failure, and the attempt is logged at `warn` under the `security` target with the realm redacted. There is deliberately no cross-host allowance and no suffix match, so a subdomain of your upstream is treated as cross-origin.

**This has a real consequence for Docker Hub — see [below](#docker-hub-pull-through-now-authenticates-anonymously).**

### 3. Proxied PyPI simple-index pages passed upstream HTML through — GHSA-4cw7-mgqj-hgmg

**The mechanism.** A proxied PyPI simple index was rewritten in place: a regular expression found `<a … href=…>` and substituted a local URL. Everything else in the upstream document survived — the only element actively removed was `<base>` (which would otherwise have re-anchored the rewritten links onto the upstream origin). A `<script>`, a `<form>`, an `<iframe>`, arbitrary wrapper markup: all forwarded verbatim and **served from your registry's own origin**. The anchor's own non-`href` attributes were re-emitted raw as well, so an upstream `onerror=` rode through untouched. And because the rewritten `href` was assembled by string interpolation, upstream-controlled bytes could break out of the attribute they were written into: a single-quoted upstream href whose fragment contains a double quote produces a rewritten anchor carrying arbitrary attacker-chosen attributes.

**Am I affected?** You need a **remote/proxy PyPI repository** (or a virtual repository with a remote PyPI member), on the per-project route `/pypi/{repo}/simple/{project}/`. Hosted repositories render their own index from database rows and were never affected, and the `/simple/` root listing was never affected either — it is rebuilt from normalized names. On a public repository the page is served to unauthenticated callers.

**Two things keep this from being as severe as "stored XSS" sounds, and both are worth stating.** First, the payload has to come from the upstream index document, so the realistic actor is a hostile or compromised private mirror, corporate index or proxied registry — **not** an ordinary package author publishing to public PyPI, which escapes its own output and enforces a filename grammar that excludes the necessary characters. Second, **script execution is blocked by the application's own Content-Security-Policy**: every response carries `script-src 'self'` with no `'unsafe-inline'`, which stops both injected `<script>` blocks and inline event handlers in any CSP-respecting browser. What was genuinely reachable is therefore stored **HTML injection** on a same-origin page — defacement, misleading content, injected form markup — rather than demonstrated script execution or session theft. That is a defence-in-depth failure worth fixing, and this is the honest size of it.

For completeness on what was *not* reachable: the pre-fix rewriter re-pointed every anchor it recognised at a local proxy path, and the breakout does not change that — so this did not let an upstream steer `pip` to fetch package bytes from an off-registry host, and the download-path gates were not bypassable this way.

**The fix** stops editing upstream markup and **rebuilds the page instead**. Each upstream anchor is parsed and a fresh minimal PEP 503 document is emitted containing only what the proxy can vouch for: one `<a>` per anchor whose href yields a usable filename, with the href rebuilt as a local `/pypi/{repo}/simple/{project}/{filename}` path plus the upstream `#fragment`; the anchor's `data-*` attributes, entity-decoded and re-escaped into fresh double-quoted values; and the escaped filename as the link text. Every other upstream byte is dropped, `<base>` among them. `data-requires-python`, the PEP 658/714 metadata attributes, `data-yanked` and the `#sha256=` fragment all survive, so `pip`'s version resolution, PEP 658 metadata fetching and hash checking are unaffected. One behaviour worth knowing: an anchor whose filename contains HTML metacharacters, whitespace or control characters is **dropped rather than escaped** — such a "filename" is a breakout payload, not a distribution name; no legal wheel or sdist filename contains those characters.

**One route is deliberately not claimed as closed.** Fetching the same index bytes through the generic download route on a remote repository — `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/download/simple/{project}/` — still streams the **raw upstream body** with the upstream's own content type and no rewriting. The CSP ceiling above applies there too, so the severity is the same rather than worse, but the class is not eliminated on that path.

### 4. Proxy-cache commits were not gated on the upstream's published digest — GHSA-qxv7-p3mq-88fv

**The mechanism.** Cargo and OCI already refused to *cache* a proxied body whose digest disagreed with the one the upstream published for it. npm, PyPI and Maven did not — each had the digest in hand and passed `None` to the cache-commit gate. So the `dist.integrity` value the server itself served in an npm packument, the `#sha256=` fragment it served in a PyPI index, and the `.sha1` sidecar it served alongside a Maven jar were all decorative on the server side: a body that disagreed with them was committed to the proxy cache and served warm from then on.

**Am I affected?** You need a **remote/proxy npm, PyPI or Maven repository**. Hosted repositories are not involved.

**Be precise about what this control is and is not** — the one-line description invites more confidence than the code earns:

- It **fails open**. No `dist.integrity` and no `shasum`, no `#sha256=` fragment, no `.sha1` sidecar — or a digest that is not in canonical bare-lowercase-hex form, or an npm SRI carrying only SHA-384 — and the fetch proceeds unverified exactly as before. The protection is only as good as the upstream's digest publication, and it degrades silently.
- On a mismatch the bytes are **still served to the client** — which verifies independently; npm checks the SRI, pip checks the hash, Maven and Gradle check the sidecar — and are only kept out of the cache. This stops persistent poisoning of the shared cache; it does not protect the client that triggered the fetch, and a plain `curl` of a proxied artifact is not protected at all.
- **How much an adversary is slowed depends on the format.** For npm and Maven the digest comes from the *same upstream over the same channel* as the artifact — the packument, the adjacent `.sha1` — so anyone who can serve you a bad tarball can serve you a matching digest; against a hostile upstream these two are near-worthless, and what they reliably catch is corruption, truncation and a broken CDN edge. PyPI is genuinely stronger: the `#sha256=` comes from the index host while the file comes from the file host, which on public PyPI is a different origin, so it catches a misbehaving or compromised file host while the index is intact. (One sharp edge shared by all three: the expected digest is itself read cache-first, so a packument, index page or sidecar already poisoned in your cache supplies the attacker's digest and the gate admits the matching bytes.)
- **Coverage inside the three formats is not total.** Repositories with scan-on-proxy enabled take a different, buffered fetch path that is not gated, and npm and Maven **virtual** repositories resolve members through an ungated entry point (PyPI virtual member fetches are gated). Maven gates **release versions only** — `-SNAPSHOT` is mutable and a racing re-deploy would pin a stale sidecar against a legitimate body — and checksum sidecars and `maven-metadata.xml` are excluded by the same rule that skips them elsewhere.
- **Three formats join three that already had it**, not all of them. OCI, Cargo and Debian were already gated; roughly twenty other proxied formats still commit to cache with no digest gate, several of them despite the upstream publishing a perfectly usable digest.
- **These mismatches do not increment the metric you may already be alerting on.** The pre-existing content-addressed gate logs under the `security` target with the repository, path and both digests, and increments `ak_proxy_cache_checksum_mismatch_total`. The new streamed gate emits a single `warn` carrying only the cache key, with no security target, no repository field and **no metric**. If you alert on that counter today, these events will not reach it.

## What to do beyond upgrading

### Rotate: upstream registry credentials, and anything presented to a plugin-served `/ext` URL

**GHSA-78h6.** If you configured upstream Basic credentials on a remote/proxy repository whose upstream you do not control, **rotate that upstream credential**. Upgrading closes the channel; it cannot un-send what may already have gone, and Basic credentials are replayable indefinitely. This is a per-upstream decision, not a blanket one — an upstream you or a trusted vendor operates over TLS is a much weaker case than a third-party registry. Repositories configured with a bearer token rather than a username and password were not exposed.

**GHSA-9rqp.** If you ran a v2 WASM protocol plugin you did not author, every credential presented to a `/ext` URL that plugin served — API tokens, session cookies, any `Authorization` header — was copied into that plugin's memory. Rotate the tokens of principals that used those routes. Keep the severity in proportion: the sandbox gives a plugin no network and no filesystem, so reading a credential and *exfiltrating* it are not the same step, and plugin installation is admin-only and signature-verified. If you author your own plugins and run nothing third-party, this is a hardening improvement rather than an incident.

### Purge: proxy-cache entries admitted before the digest gate existed

**GHSA-qxv7.** Nothing in this release evicts or revalidates what is already cached: there is no migration, no startup revalidation, no backfill. Any npm tarball, PyPI distribution or Maven release artifact whose bytes disagreed with its published digest and was cached before the upgrade **stays cached and keeps being served warm**. Upgrading stops new ones being admitted.

**Do not expect this to age out.** Proxied package files are classified immutable, which means their cache entries are always evaluated fresh, carry a ten-year backstop TTL, and are never revalidated against upstream again. A bad entry sits there until someone removes it.

Removing one is explicit and per-path. Enumerate a remote repository's cached entries with `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts` — the listing carries each entry's `path`, `size_bytes` and stored `checksum_sha256` — and evict with `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/cache/invalidate?path=<path>` for each. That call needs `repository:admin` on the repository, takes **one path at a time** (there is no prefix, glob or bulk form), and hard-deletes the body, its metadata sidecar and the catalog row. The only whole-repository purge in the codebase runs on repository deletion, so a genuinely clean slate means deleting and recreating the remote repository.

Whether to purge is a judgement call, and a cheap one to get wrong in the safe direction — proxy-cache entries are re-fetchable from upstream by definition, so evicting costs bandwidth and a cold first pull, not data. If you have any reason to suspect a bad entry — a corrupted-install report, a flaky upstream or mirror, an upstream incident inside your retention window — evict and let it re-populate under the new gate. With no such signal, taking the fix going forward is defensible.

**GHSA-4cw7 needs no purge, and it is worth saying so explicitly** given the manual loop above. The proxy caches the raw upstream index body and the page is rebuilt in the handler on **every** serve, warm cache hits included — so a poisoned index cached before the upgrade is sanitized on read the moment you deploy. There is nothing to evict.

### Docker Hub pull-through now authenticates anonymously

This is the one deliberate behaviour change in the release, and it is a consequence of the GHSA-78h6 fix rather than a separate decision.

Docker Hub splits its registry and its token endpoint across two hosts: pulls go to `registry-1.docker.io`, while the realm it advertises is `auth.docker.io`. Under the strict origin rule those are **different origins**, so a Docker Hub remote repository with configured credentials now performs its token exchange **without them**.

Docker Hub does not reject that request — it answers with a valid *anonymous-scope* token. Two consequences follow:

- **Private Docker Hub images stop being pullable** through that repository. The anonymous token is accepted by the token endpoint and then refused by the registry on the retry, so **the failure surfaces one hop later as an upstream error (`502 Upstream returned error status 401`), not as an authentication failure.** If you hit this after upgrading, that misleading error is the signature — the fix is to stop proxying private Docker Hub content through a credentialed remote, not to re-check your Docker Hub password.
- **Pulls fall under Docker Hub's anonymous rate limits** rather than your account's. On a busy CI fleet that is the effect you will notice first.

**Am I affected?** Only if you proxy an upstream whose token realm lives on a different host from the registry itself *and* you configured credentials on that repository. Docker Hub is the common case. Registries that advertise a same-origin realm — GHCR serves pulls from `ghcr.io` and advertises `ghcr.io/token`, as do most self-hosted Harbor, Nexus and Artifactory deployments — are unaffected and keep authenticating exactly as before. Check your own upstreams against that rule rather than assuming; the realm host is in the `WWW-Authenticate` header of an unauthenticated `GET` against the upstream's `/v2/`.

There is no configuration switch to opt back in. The trade is deliberate: this codebase pins credentials to the operator-configured origin everywhere, and a cross-host allowance would reopen the advisory for every upstream that has one.

## Can I tell whether this happened to me?

Mostly not, and where the answer is no it is worth saying so rather than leaving you to search for a log line that was never written. One of the four does support a real check.

- **GHSA-9rqp** — **no.** There is no audit record, no download-statistics row, and no distinguishing log line: a successful `/ext` request writes no audit entry, never reaches the download-event path, and emits nothing at the default `info` log level. Request metrics label by matched route (`/ext/:format_key/:repo_key/*path`), so they carry neither the repository key nor the principal. Even with an external reverse-proxy access log, an exploiting request is byte-identical in shape to a legitimate one — same method, same URL — and the only thing that distinguishes them is which grants the caller held, which nothing records. **If the affected configuration was present, treat those repositories' inventories as potentially disclosed.**
- **GHSA-78h6** — **not from a normal deployment.** The realm that was contacted was recorded only at `debug`, and the shipped container image pins `RUST_LOG=info`, so a production instance emitted nothing; no metric and no stored record retains it either, and the token cache is in-memory. A successful exfiltration is silent by construction — an attacker returning a well-formed token produces no error line. (A deployment running the development compose defaults *did* log the realm at debug, so if that is you and you still hold the logs, they are worth a look.) Going forward, the new cross-origin refusal *is* logged at `warn` under the `security` target — useful for spotting the Docker Hub behaviour change above, but it says nothing about the past. The practical assessment is the configuration review described earlier, not a log search.
- **GHSA-4cw7** — **you can check what is cached now, not what was served.** The proxy caches the raw upstream body, so a currently-cached index page can be inspected directly: on filesystem storage the bodies sit at `<storage>/proxy-cache/<repo_key>/simple/<project>/__content__`, on S3/GCS under the same key prefix at bucket root, and `proxy_cache_artifacts` lets you enumerate them first. Grep those for `<script`, `onerror=` and similar. What no record answers is whether a poisoned page was *ever served* — upstream response bodies are never logged. Absence of evidence is weak evidence here.
- **GHSA-qxv7** — **yes, with an offline check, and this is the one place a query helps.** Every cached entry stores a `checksum_sha256` in its metadata sidecar and in the `proxy_cache_artifacts` catalog, surfaced by `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts`. For **PyPI** that stored value is directly comparable to the `#sha256=` fragment the upstream index advertises for the same filename — pull the listing, fetch the upstream index, diff, no artifact re-download needed. For **npm** and **Maven** the published digests are SHA-512 and SHA-1, so the stored SHA-256 is not comparable and you must re-hash the cached object to compare. The caveat that keeps this honest: you are comparing against *today's* upstream digest, so this detects divergence rather than proving what happened at the time — against an upstream that was compromised and has since been corrected it finds the bad entry; against one still serving the attacker's digest it will not.

## What's Changed

**Security**

- Resolve the repository key from the third path segment on `/ext` WASM proxy routes, enforce `require_visible` in the handler, and allowlist the headers forwarded into plugin memory (GHSA-9rqp-mgmw-5879)
- Pin OCI bearer-realm credential forwarding to the configured upstream's origin (GHSA-78h6-3wp8-2542)
- Rebuild proxied PyPI simple-index pages from parsed anchors instead of forwarding upstream HTML (GHSA-4cw7-mgqj-hgmg)
- Gate npm, PyPI and Maven proxy-cache commits on the upstream's published digest (GHSA-qxv7-p3mq-88fv)

All four ship in a single commit — https://github.com/artifact-keeper/artifact-keeper/pull/3347

See the [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md) for the itemized entries with the mechanism behind each one.
